title: Das Eselein
source: Brüder Grimm, Kinder- und Hausmärchen, Band 2, 7. Auflage (Ausgabe letzter Hand), Dieterich, Göttingen 1857, KHM 144. Text from Wikisource (twice proofread against the original). Fresh translation made directly from the German; 1857 spelling preserved (daß, gieng, fieng, Thür, Rath). The 1857 edition prints this tale without paragraph breaks; the paragraphing here is editorial, added for readability. The wording is unchanged.
about: KHM 144: a queen's prayer for a child is answered with a donkey rather than a son, and the little donkey — clever, musical, and ashamed of his own reflection — is raised as heir before setting off into the world to make his own fortune. At a foreign court he wins a princess's hand and sheds his hide by night in secret, until her father burns it and forces his true shape to stay for good. It belongs to the same family as the frog king and the bearskin bridegroom: the animal husband disenchanted by force, not by tenderness.

sentences.t: Es lebte einmal ein König und eine Königin, die waren reich und hatten alles, was sie sich wünschten, nur keine Kinder.
sentences.l: There lived once a king and a queen, they were rich and had everything that they wished for themselves, only no children.
sentences.i: There once lived a king and a queen; they were rich and had everything they could wish for, only no children.
sentences.n: Nothing divides this tale in the 1857 book — it stands as one block from beginning to end; the paragraph breaks here have been added for the reader’s eye, and the German itself is untouched. die waren is a demonstrative, not a relative: the sentence starts fresh, “they were rich,” the way spoken narrative does. “sich etwas wünschen” puts the person in the dative — what they wished for themselves.

sentences.t: Darüber klagte sie Tag und Nacht und sprach „ich bin wie ein Acker, auf dem nichts wächst.“
sentences.l: About that she lamented day and night and spoke “I am like a field on which nothing grows.”
sentences.i: Over that she lamented day and night, and said: “I am like a field where nothing grows.”
sentences.n: darüber = über das, about that; German gathers a preposition and its pronoun into one word of this kind constantly. “Tag und Nacht” stands bare, without articles, as in English. sprach is this teller’s verb for said, and it will recur on nearly every page.

sentences.t: Endlich erfüllte Gott ihre Wünsche: als das Kind aber zur Welt kam, sahs nicht aus wie ein Menschenkind, sondern war ein junges Eselein.
sentences.l: At last God fulfilled her wishes: but when the child came to the world, it looked not out like a human child, but was a young little donkey.
sentences.i: At last God granted her wishes; but when the child came into the world it did not look like a human child, but was a young little donkey.
sentences.n: “zur Welt kommen” = to be born. sahs is sah es with the pronoun swallowed into the verb, which the 1857 text does often; the verb itself is aussehen, to look, and its particle aus stands at the end. Eselein is a diminutive and neuter — which is why the tale calls its prince es, “it,” for pages to come.

sentences.t: Wie die Mutter das erblickte, fieng ihr Jammer und Geschrei erst recht an, sie hätte lieber gar kein Kind gehabt als einen Esel,
sentences.l: When the mother caught sight of that, her wailing and crying began only then in earnest, she would rather have had no child at all than a donkey,
sentences.i: When the mother saw it, her wailing and crying began in earnest: she would rather have had no child at all than a donkey,
sentences.n: wie here is “when,” not “how.” fieng … an is anfangen with its particle carried to the far end of the clause, and fieng is the 1857 spelling of fing. “erst recht” = all the more, now in good earnest. hätte … gehabt is the subjunctive of what she would have preferred.

sentences.t: und sagte man sollt ihn ins Wasser werfen, damit ihn die Fische fräßen.
sentences.l: and said one should throw him into the water, so that the fishes might devour him.
sentences.i: and said he should be thrown into the water for the fishes to devour.
sentences.n: Reported speech with no daß: “sagte man sollt ihn werfen.” sollt is the older short form of sollte. fräßen is the subjunctive of fressen, the verb German keeps for animals feeding — the mother’s wish is exact and ugly, and the tale does not soften it.

sentences.t: Der König aber sprach „nein, hat Gott ihn gegeben, soll er auch mein Sohn und Erbe sein, nach meinem Tod auf dem königlichen Thron sitzen und die königliche Krone tragen.“
sentences.l: The king however spoke “no, has God given him, he shall also be my son and heir, after my death sit on the royal throne and wear the royal crown.”
sentences.i: But the king said: “No — if God has given him, then he shall be my son and heir too, and after my death sit on the royal throne and wear the royal crown.”
sentences.n: “hat Gott ihn gegeben” is a conditional clause with no wenn: German can put the verb first and mean “if …”. Thron, like Thür and Thier later, is the 1857 th- spelling. tragen with a crown is to wear it, not to carry it.

sentences.t: Also ward das Eselein aufgezogen, nahm zu, und die Ohren wuchsen ihm auch fein hoch und gerad hinauf.
sentences.l: So was the little donkey reared, it grew, and the ears grew on it too, fine and high and straight up.
sentences.i: So the little donkey was reared and thrived, and its ears grew up fine and high and straight.
sentences.n: ward is the old form of wurde and carries most of the passives in this tale. zunehmen, here “nahm zu,” is to increase, to put on growth. “die Ohren wuchsen ihm” is the dative of possession: German says the ears grew to him where English says his ears grew.

sentences.t: Es war aber sonst fröhlicher Art, sprang herum, spielte und hatte besonders seine Lust an der Musik,
sentences.l: It was however otherwise of cheerful kind, sprang about, played and had especially its delight in music,
sentences.i: For the rest it was of a cheerful nature, leapt about, played, and had its particular delight in music,
sentences.n: “fröhlicher Art” is a bare genitive of description — of a cheerful sort — where modern German would put von in front of it. “seine Lust an etwas haben” = to take one’s pleasure in a thing.

sentences.t: so daß es zu einem berühmten Spielmann gieng und sprach „lehre mich deine Kunst, daß ich so gut die Laute schlagen kann als du.“
sentences.l: so that it went to a famous minstrel and spoke “teach me your art, that I can strike the lute as well as you.”
sentences.i: so that it went to a famous minstrel and said: “Teach me your art, so that I can play the lute as well as you.”
sentences.n: lehre is the imperative of lehren, to teach — not die Lehre, a lesson, which is what this spelling means elsewhere in the collection. German strikes a lute, “die Laute schlagen,” rather than playing it. “so gut … als” is the older comparison where modern German says wie.

sentences.t: „Ach, liebes Herrlein,“ antwortete der Spielmann, „das sollt euch schwer fallen, eure Finger sind nicht allerdings dazu gemacht und gar zu groß; ich sorge die Saiten haltens nicht aus.“
sentences.l: “Ah, dear little lord,” answered the minstrel, “that would fall hard for you, your fingers are not exactly made for it and much too big; I fear the strings will not hold it out.”
sentences.i: “Ah, dear young master,” answered the minstrel, “that would come hard to you; your fingers are not altogether made for it, and far too large. I am afraid the strings will not stand it.”
sentences.n: euch and eure are the older respectful address, like French vous; in English they are still simply “you” and “your.” “schwer fallen” = to come hard to someone. ich sorge is the verb sorgen, I fear — not die Sorge, a worry. haltens is halten es with the pronoun attached, and the aus at the end makes the verb aushalten, to hold out.

sentences.t: Es half keine Ausrede, das Eselein wollte und mußte die Laute schlagen, war beharrlich und fleißig, und lernte es am Ende so gut als sein Meister selber.
sentences.l: There helped no excuse, the little donkey wanted and had to strike the lute, was persistent and diligent, and learnt it in the end as well as its master himself.
sentences.i: No excuse was any use: the little donkey would and must play the lute, and it was dogged and diligent, and learnt it in the end as well as its master himself.
sentences.n: “es half keine Ausrede” — no getting out of it; helfen is impersonal here, with the excuse as subject. “wollte und mußte” sets two modals side by side and lets them share the one infinitive.

sentences.t: Einmal gieng das junge Herrlein nachdenksam spazieren und kam an einen Brunnen, da schaute es hinein und sah im spiegelhellen Wasser seine Eseleinsgestalt.
sentences.l: Once went the young little lord pensively for a walk and came to a well, there it looked in and saw in the mirror-bright water its donkey’s-shape.
sentences.i: One day the young master went out walking, deep in thought, and came to a well; he looked in, and saw in the mirror-bright water his donkey’s shape.
sentences.n: “spazieren gehen” is a fixed pair, to go for a walk. “an einen Brunnen” with the accusative is motion up to it, not rest beside it. da is “there, at that point,” and being first it pushes the verb ahead of the subject: schaute es.

sentences.t: Darüber war es so betrübt, daß es in die weite Welt gieng und nur einen treuen Gesellen mitnahm.
sentences.l: About that it was so grieved that it went into the wide world and took along only one faithful companion.
sentences.i: Over that he was so grieved that he went out into the wide world and took only one faithful companion with him.
sentences.n: “in die weite Welt gehen” is the collection’s formula for leaving home for good. mitnahm is mitnehmen with the particle rejoined at the end of the clause.

sentences.t: Sie zogen auf und ab, zuletzt kamen sie in ein Reich, wo ein alter König herrschte, der nur eine einzige aber wunderschöne Tochter hatte.
sentences.l: They travelled up and down, at the last they came into a kingdom where an old king ruled, who had only a single but wondrously beautiful daughter.
sentences.i: They travelled up and down, and at last came into a kingdom where an old king ruled, who had one daughter only, but she was wondrously beautiful.
sentences.n: ziehen in these tales is to travel, to journey, never to pull; “auf und ab” is up and down the country. Reich here is the noun, a kingdom — the same spelling is also the adjective rich, which is what it meant in the tale’s first line.

sentences.t: Das Eselein sagte „hier wollen wir weilen,“ klopfte ans Thor und rief „es ist ein Gast haußen, macht auf, damit er eingehen kann.“
sentences.l: The little donkey said “here will we tarry,” knocked at the gate and cried “there is a guest outside, open up, so that he can go in.”
sentences.i: The little donkey said, “Here we will stay,” knocked at the gate and called: “There is a guest outside — open, so that he may come in.”
sentences.n: haußen is the older word for draußen, outside, still heard in the south. “macht auf” is aufmachen, open up, in the plural imperative thrown at whoever is behind the gate. eingehen here means plainly to go in; its modern senses came later.

sentences.t: Als aber nicht aufgethan ward, setzte er sich hin, nahm seine Laute und schlug sie mit seinen zwei Vorderfüßen aufs lieblichste.
sentences.l: But when there was not opened, he set himself down, took his lute and struck it with his two forefeet in the loveliest way.
sentences.i: But when nobody opened, he sat himself down, took his lute and played it with his two forefeet in the loveliest manner.
sentences.n: An impersonal passive with no subject at all — “als nicht aufgethan ward,” when there was no opening — which German can do and English cannot. aufgethan is the 1857 spelling of aufgetan. “aufs lieblichste” = in the loveliest way. From here on the tale begins to say er of the donkey where it had said es.

sentences.t: Da sperrte der Thürhüter gewaltig die Augen auf, lief zum König und sprach „da draußen sitzt ein junges Eselein vor dem Thor, das schlägt die Laute so gut als ein gelernter Meister.“
sentences.l: Then opened the door-keeper his eyes mightily wide, ran to the king and spoke “out there sits a young little donkey before the gate, it strikes the lute as well as a trained master.”
sentences.i: Then the door-keeper opened his eyes wide indeed, ran to the king and said: “Out there before the gate sits a young little donkey, and it plays the lute as well as a master of the trade.”
sentences.n: “die Augen aufsperren” is to open the eyes wide: sperren by itself means to shut or to bar, and only the particle auf turns it round. ein gelernter Meister is one who has served his years at a craft, not a learned man.

sentences.t: „So laß mir den Musikant hereinkommen“ sprach der König.
sentences.l: “So let me the musician come in” spoke the king.
sentences.i: “Then let the musician come in to me,” said the king.
sentences.n: mir is the ethical dative: it slips the speaker’s own interest into the order — let him come in, for me — and English has no word for it. Musikant is a player of instruments, and the word can carry a slight condescension.

sentences.t: Wie aber ein Eselein hereintrat, fieng alles an über den Lautenschläger zu lachen.
sentences.l: But when a little donkey stepped in, everything began to laugh over the lute-striker.
sentences.i: But when a little donkey walked in, everyone began to laugh at the lute-player.
sentences.n: alles for “everybody” — the neuter takes in the whole company at once. “über jemanden lachen” = to laugh at someone. Lautenschläger is built as the German idiom is: the one who strikes the lute.

sentences.t: Nun sollte das Eselein unten zu den Knechten gesetzt und gespeist werden, es ward aber unwillig und sprach „ich bin kein gemeines Stalleselein, ich bin ein vornehmes.“
sentences.l: Now was the little donkey to be seated and fed below among the servants, but it became indignant and spoke “I am no common stable-donkey, I am a grand one.”
sentences.i: Now the little donkey was to be seated below with the farmhands and fed there; but it grew indignant and said: “I am no common stable donkey, I am one of high birth.”
sentences.n: unten is below the salt — where the household servants ate, away from the king’s own table. vornehmes is an adjective standing on its own as a noun, and it is neuter because Eselein is neuter.

sentences.t: Da sagten sie „wenn du das bist, so setze dich zu dem Kriegsvolk.“
sentences.l: Then said they “if you are that, so seat yourself with the fighting men.”
sentences.i: Then they said: “If that is what you are, sit with the soldiers.”
sentences.n: setze dich is the imperative of sich setzen, to seat oneself. Kriegsvolk is a collective and singular in German — the fighting men of the household, a rank above the servants and below the king.

sentences.t: „Nein,“ sprach es, „ich will beim König sitzen.“
sentences.l: “No,” it spoke, “I want to sit by the king.”
sentences.i: “No,” it said, “I will sit by the king.”
sentences.n: wollen is to want, to be set on a thing: “ich will” is not the English future but a declaration of intent. beim = bei dem.

sentences.t: Der König lachte und sprach in gutem Muth „ja, es soll so sein, wie du verlangst, Eselein, komm her zu mir.“
sentences.l: The king laughed and spoke in good spirits “yes, it shall be so as you ask, little donkey, come here to me.”
sentences.i: The king laughed and said in good humour: “Yes, it shall be as you ask, little donkey — come here to me.”
sentences.n: “in gutem Muth” = in good spirits; Muth is the 1857 spelling of Mut. verlangen is to ask for, to demand — it comes back twice more, and each time it is the donkey doing the asking.

sentences.t: Danach fragte er „Eselein, wie gefällt dir meine Tochter?“
sentences.l: After that asked he “little donkey, how pleases you my daughter?”
sentences.i: After that he asked: “Little donkey, how do you like my daughter?”
sentences.n: German turns the question round: the daughter does the pleasing and the person stands in the dative — “wie gefällt dir …” for “how do you like …”.

sentences.t: Das Eselein drehte den Kopf nach ihr, schaute sie an, nickte und sprach „aus der Maßen wohl, sie ist so schön wie ich noch keine gesehen habe.“
sentences.l: The little donkey turned the head toward her, looked at her, nodded and spoke “out of measure well, she is so beautiful as I have yet seen none.”
sentences.i: The little donkey turned its head towards her, looked at her, nodded and said: “Beyond all measure — she is fairer than any I have ever seen.”
sentences.n: “aus der Maßen” is the old phrase for beyond measure, exceedingly. “den Kopf drehen” takes the plain article where English takes a possessive, its head. schaute … an is anschauen split around its object.

sentences.t: „Nun, so sollst du auch neben ihr sitzen“ sagte der König.
sentences.l: “Well, so you shall also sit beside her” said the king.
sentences.i: “Well then, you shall sit beside her too,” said the king.
sentences.n: sollen here is the king’s decree — you shall — and not a way of forming the future.

sentences.t: „Das ist mir eben recht“ sprach das Eselein und setzte sich an ihre Seite, aß und trank und wußte sich fein und säuberlich zu betragen.
sentences.l: “That is to me just right” spoke the little donkey and set itself at her side, ate and drank and knew how to conduct itself finely and neatly.
sentences.i: “That suits me exactly,” said the little donkey, and sat down at her side, ate and drank, and knew how to conduct itself daintily and cleanly.
sentences.n: “das ist mir recht” = that suits me, with eben sharpening it to exactly. “wissen zu” with an infinitive is to know how to do a thing. sich betragen is to conduct oneself — the word a court uses of manners, and the tale is watching the donkey’s.

sentences.t: Als das edle Thierlein eine gute Zeit an des Königs Hof geblieben war, dachte es „was hilft das alles, du mußt wieder heim,“ ließ den Kopf traurig hängen, trat vor den König und verlangte seinen Abschied.
sentences.l: When the noble little creature had stayed a good while at the king’s court, it thought “what helps all that, you must go home again,” let the head hang sadly, stepped before the king and asked for its leave.
sentences.i: When the noble little creature had stayed a good while at the king’s court, it thought: “What use is all this — you must go home again,” let its head hang sadly, stepped before the king and asked leave to go.
sentences.n: It says du to itself, which German thought does freely: you must go home. “des Königs Hof” puts the genitive before its noun, an older and more elevated order than “der Hof des Königs.” “den Kopf hängen lassen” = to let the head droop, to go about downcast. Abschied is the leave a servant or a soldier is given when he departs.

sentences.t: Der König hatte es aber lieb gewonnen und sprach „Eselein was ist dir? du schaust ja sauer wie ein Essigkrug: bleib bei mir, ich will dir geben, was du verlangst. Willst du Gold?“
sentences.l: But the king had grown fond of it and spoke “little donkey what is to you? you look indeed sour as a vinegar jug: stay with me, I will give you what you ask. Do you want gold?”
sentences.i: But the king had grown fond of it, and said: “Little donkey, what is the matter with you? You look as sour as a vinegar jug. Stay with me — I will give you whatever you ask. Do you want gold?”
sentences.n: “lieb gewinnen” = to grow fond of. “was ist dir?” is the plain German for what ails you, with the person in the dative. ja inside a sentence is not “yes” but a nudge — you do look sour.

sentences.t: „Nein“ sagte das Eselein und schüttelte mit dem Kopf.
sentences.l: “No” said the little donkey and shook with the head.
sentences.i: “No,” said the little donkey, and shook its head.
sentences.n: German shakes with the head — “mit dem Kopf schütteln” — where English shakes the head itself.

sentences.t: „Willst du Kostbarkeiten und Schmuck?“ „Nein.“
sentences.l: “Do you want treasures and jewellery?” “No.”
sentences.i: “Do you want treasures and finery?” “No.”
sentences.n: The offers and refusals run on with no speech tags at all: the 1857 text simply sets them one after another and lets the reader keep count.

sentences.t: „Willst du mein halbes Reich?“ „Ach nein.“
sentences.l: “Do you want my half kingdom?” “Ah no.”
sentences.i: “Will you have half my kingdom?” “Ah, no.”
sentences.n: “mein halbes Reich” carries the half inside the phrase as an adjective, my half kingdom. Half a kingdom is the standard reward of these tales, and the refusal of it is the point of the scene.

sentences.t: Da sprach der König „wenn ich nur wüßte was dich vergnügt machen könnte: willst du meine schöne Tochter zur Frau?“
sentences.l: Then spoke the king “if I only knew what could make you content: do you want my beautiful daughter for a wife?”
sentences.i: Then the king said: “If only I knew what could make you content — will you have my beautiful daughter for a wife?”
sentences.n: wüßte and könnte are subjunctives of the unreal wish, and wüßte is the 1857 spelling of wüsste. “zur Frau” = zu der Frau: German marks the role with zu where English says for.

sentences.t: „Ach ja,“ sagte das Eselein, „die möchte ich wohl haben,“ war auf einmal ganz lustig und guter Dinge, denn das wars gerade, was es sich gewünscht hatte.
sentences.l: “Ah yes,” said the little donkey, “that one I would like to have,” was all at once quite merry and of good things, for that was exactly what it had wished itself.
sentences.i: “Ah yes,” said the little donkey, “her I should like to have” — and it was all at once quite merry and in high spirits, for that was the very thing it had wished for.
sentences.n: die at the head of the clause is the demonstrative, her, that one, put first for emphasis. “guter Dinge sein” is a fixed phrase for being in high spirits — literally of good things. wars is war es.

sentences.t: Also ward eine große und prächtige Hochzeit gehalten.
sentences.l: So was a great and splendid wedding held.
sentences.i: So a great and splendid wedding was held.
sentences.n: also = thus, so, and never English “also.” The line is a passive with ward, and the tale gives the wedding one sentence and moves straight on to the night.

sentences.t: Abends, wie Braut und Bräutigam in ihr Schlafkämmerlein geführt wurden, wollte der König wissen ob sich das Eselein auch fein artig und manierlich betrüge, und hieß einem Diener sich dort verstecken.
sentences.l: In the evening, when bride and bridegroom were led into their little bedchamber, wanted the king to know whether the little donkey behaved itself properly and mannerly, and bade a servant hide himself there.
sentences.i: In the evening, when bride and bridegroom were led to their bedchamber, the king wanted to know whether the little donkey would behave itself decently and with good manners, and bade a servant hide himself in there.
sentences.n: betrüge is the subjunctive of reported wondering — how it might behave — and belongs to sich betragen, to conduct oneself, not to betrügen, to deceive. heißen with the person in the dative is to bid someone do a thing. Kämmerlein is a diminutive built on Kammer, a chamber made small and cosy.

sentences.t: Wie sie nun beide drinnen waren, schob der Bräutigam den Riegel vor die Thüre, blickte sich um,
sentences.l: When they were now both inside, pushed the bridegroom the bolt before the door, looked himself around,
sentences.i: When the two of them were inside, the bridegroom pushed the bolt across the door, looked about him,
sentences.n: “den Riegel vorschieben” is to shoot the bolt. “sich umblicken” is reflexive in German — he looks himself around — where English just looks around.

sentences.t: und wie er glaubte daß sie ganz allein wären, da warf er auf einmal seine Eselshaut ab und stand da als ein schöner königlicher Jüngling.
sentences.l: and when he believed that they were quite alone, then threw he off all at once his donkey’s skin and stood there as a fair royal youth.
sentences.i: and when he believed they were quite alone, he threw off his donkey’s skin all at once and stood there a fair and kingly youth.
sentences.n: wären is subjunctive because it is what he believed, not what the teller asserts. abwerfen is to throw off, its ab held back to the end of the clause — the hinge of the whole tale rests on that one particle.

sentences.t: „Nun siehst du,“ sprach er, „wer ich bin, und siehst auch daß ich deiner nicht unwerth war.“
sentences.l: “Now you see,” he spoke, “who I am, and see also that I was not unworthy of you.”
sentences.i: “Now you see,” he said, “who I am; and you see too that I was not unworthy of you.”
sentences.n: deiner is the genitive of du, governed by unwerth: German says unworthy of-you with a case where English needs a preposition. unwerth is the 1857 spelling of unwert. Husband and wife say du to each other, and du is “you.”

sentences.t: Da ward die Braut froh, küßte ihn und hatte ihn von Herzen lieb.
sentences.l: Then became the bride glad, kissed him and had him dear from the heart.
sentences.i: Then the bride was glad, kissed him, and loved him with all her heart.
sentences.n: “jemanden lieb haben” is this collection’s ordinary way of saying to love someone; “von Herzen” = from the heart, heartily.

sentences.t: Als aber der Morgen herankam, sprang er auf, zog seine Thierhaut wieder über, und hätte kein Mensch gedacht was für einer dahinter steckte.
sentences.l: But when the morning came on, he sprang up, pulled his animal skin over again, and would no man have thought what sort of one was stuck behind it.
sentences.i: But when morning came he sprang up, drew his beast’s hide on again, and no one would have guessed what manner of man was hidden behind it.
sentences.n: überziehen, to pull a thing on over oneself, splits: “zog … über.” “was für einer” = what kind of a one. “dahinter stecken” is to be behind a thing, to lie concealed in it, and it is still the everyday German for what is really going on.

sentences.t: Bald kam auch der alte König gegangen, „ei,“ rief er, „ist das Eselein schon munter!
sentences.l: Soon came also the old king walking, “ei,” cried he, “is the little donkey already awake!
sentences.i: Soon the old king came walking in as well. “Well now,” he cried, “is the little donkey awake already!
sentences.n: “kam gegangen” — German pairs kommen with a past participle to say how someone came: came walking. ei is a soft interjection, well now. The exclamation is punctuated as an exclamation though it asks a question, and the 1857 text is kept as it stands.

sentences.t: Du bist wohl recht traurig,“ sagte er zu seiner Tochter, „daß du keinen ordentlichen Menschen zum Mann bekommen hast?“
sentences.l: You are surely quite sad,” said he to his daughter, “that you have got no proper human being for a husband?”
sentences.i: You must be sorry indeed,” he said to his daughter, “that you have got no proper man for a husband?”
sentences.n: The king’s speech runs on across the speech tag, so its opening quotation mark stands back in the line before. wohl here is “I suppose, surely” — a guess, not “well.” “zum Mann bekommen” = to get as a husband. Mensch is a human being, and that is the whole point of the question.

sentences.t: „Ach nein, lieber Vater, ich habe ihn so lieb, als wenn er der allerschönste wäre, und will ihn mein Lebtag behalten.“
sentences.l: “Ah no, dear father, I have him as dear as if he were the very fairest, and want to keep him my life-day.”
sentences.i: “Ah no, dear father, I love him as if he were the fairest of all, and I mean to keep him as long as I live.”
sentences.n: “als wenn … wäre” is the unreal comparison, as if he were. “mein Lebtag” is an old bare accusative of time: for my whole life long.

sentences.t: Der König wunderte sich, aber der Diener, der sich versteckt hatte, kam und offenbarte ihm alles.
sentences.l: The king wondered himself, but the servant, who had hidden himself, came and revealed him everything.
sentences.i: The king was astonished; but the servant who had hidden himself came and disclosed it all to him.
sentences.n: “sich wundern” is reflexive in German: to be surprised. offenbaren is the elevated word for disclosing what was hidden, and the tale keeps it for the one moment the secret is told.

sentences.t: Der König sprach „das ist nimmermehr wahr.“
sentences.l: The king spoke “that is nevermore true.”
sentences.i: The king said: “That can never be true.”
sentences.n: nimmermehr is the old strong never — not “never again” here but “never in the world.”

sentences.t: „So wacht selber die folgende Nacht, ihr werdets mit eigenen Augen sehen,
sentences.l: “So keep watch yourself the following night, you will see it with your own eyes,
sentences.i: “Then keep watch yourself the next night, and you will see it with your own eyes,
sentences.n: wacht is the plural imperative of wachen, to keep watch — not die Wacht, a watch or guard. The servant says ihr to the king, the older respectful address, which is still “you.” werdets is werdet es with the pronoun swallowed. “die folgende Nacht” stands in the bare accusative of time, with no preposition at all.

sentences.t: und wißt ihr was, Herr König, nehmt ihm die Haut weg und werft sie ins Feuer, so muß er sich wohl in seiner rechten Gestalt zeigen.“
sentences.l: and know you what, my lord king, take the skin away from him and throw it into the fire, then must he surely show himself in his right shape.”
sentences.i: and do you know what, my lord king — take the skin away from him and throw it into the fire, and then he must show himself in his true shape.”
sentences.n: “wißt ihr was” is thrown in as English throws in “I tell you what.” “nehmt ihm die Haut weg” has the dative of the person robbed: take from him the skin. wegnehmen and werfen both stand in the plural imperative, matching the ihr.

sentences.t: „Dein Rath ist gut“ sprach der König,
sentences.l: “Your counsel is good” spoke the king,
sentences.i: “Your counsel is good,” said the king,
sentences.n: Rath is the 1857 spelling of Rat, counsel or advice. The servant says du to the king in one breath and ihr in the next; both are “you” in English, and the wavering is the servant’s, not a mistake.

sentences.t: und Abends als sie schliefen, schlich er sich hinein, und wie er zum Bett kam, sah er im Mondschein einen stolzen Jüngling da ruhen, und die Haut lag abgestreift auf der Erde.
sentences.l: and in the evening when they slept, he crept himself in, and when he came to the bed, he saw in the moonlight a proud youth resting there, and the skin lay stripped off on the ground.
sentences.i: and in the evening, when they were asleep, he crept in; and when he came to the bed he saw by moonlight a proud young man lying there at rest, and the skin lay stripped off on the floor.
sentences.n: “sich schleichen” is reflexive — he crept himself in. “sah … ruhen” uses the bare infinitive after a verb of perceiving, as English says saw him rest. abgestreift, the past participle of abstreifen, describes how the skin lay: stripped off, like something shed.

sentences.t: Da nahm er sie weg und ließ draußen ein gewaltiges Feuer anmachen und die Haut hineinwerfen, und blieb selber dabei, bis sie ganz zu Asche verbrannt war.
sentences.l: Then took he it away and had outside a mighty fire kindled and the skin thrown in, and stayed himself by it, until it was quite burnt to ashes.
sentences.i: Then he took it away and had a great fire kindled outside and the skin thrown into it, and stayed by it himself until it was burnt quite to ashes.
sentences.n: lassen with an infinitive is to have a thing done: the king lights nothing himself. sie is the skin, feminine in German and “it” in English. He stays to the end, which is how the tale marks that this is deliberate and not an accident.

sentences.t: Weil er aber sehen wollte wie sich der Beraubte anstellen würde, blieb er die Nacht über wach und lauschte.
sentences.l: But because he wanted to see how the robbed one would carry himself, he stayed the night through awake and listened.
sentences.i: But because he wanted to see how the man he had robbed would take it, he stayed awake all night and listened.
sentences.n: “sich anstellen” is to behave, to take a thing — not anstellen, to set up or arrange. der Beraubte is a participle made into a noun, the robbed one; German forms such nouns freely. “die Nacht über” = through the night.

sentences.t: Als der Jüngling ausgeschlafen hatte, beim ersten Morgenschein, stand er auf und wollte die Eselshaut anziehen, aber sie war nicht zu finden.
sentences.l: When the youth had slept himself out, at the first light of morning, he stood up and wanted to put on the donkey’s skin, but it was not to find.
sentences.i: When the young man had slept his fill, at the first light of morning, he got up and wanted to put on the donkey’s skin, but it was nowhere to be found.
sentences.n: ausschlafen is to sleep as long as one needs. “sie war nicht zu finden” — sein with zu and an infinitive says a thing can be done, or here that it cannot: it was not to be found.

sentences.t: Da erschrack er und sprach voll Trauer und Angst „nun muß ich sehen daß ich entfliehe.“
sentences.l: Then took he fright and spoke full of grief and fear “now I must see that I get away.”
sentences.i: Then he took fright, and said, full of grief and fear: “Now I must see to it that I escape.”
sentences.n: erschrack is the 1857 spelling of erschrak, the past of erschrecken in its intransitive sense, to take fright. “sehen daß …” is the same idiom English has: to see to it that.

sentences.t: Wie er hinaustrat, stand aber der König da und sprach „mein Sohn, wohin so eilig, was hast du im Sinn?
sentences.l: When he stepped out, stood however the king there and spoke “my son, whither so hastily, what have you in mind?
sentences.i: But when he stepped outside, there stood the king, and said: “My son, where away in such haste? What have you in mind?
sentences.n: hinaustreten is to step out, away from where the speaker stands. The king calls him mein Sohn before anything else is said, and the whole ending follows from that one word. “im Sinn haben” = to have in mind, to intend.

sentences.t: Bleib hier, du bist ein so schöner Mann, du sollst nicht wieder von mir. Ich gebe dir jetzt mein Reich halb, und nach meinem Tod bekommst du es ganz.“
sentences.l: Stay here, you are so fair a man, you shall not [go] from me again. I give you now my kingdom half, and after my death you get it whole.”
sentences.i: Stay here — you are so fine a man; you shall not leave me again. I give you half my kingdom now, and after my death you shall have it whole.”
sentences.n: “du sollst nicht wieder von mir” leaves the verb of motion out altogether, and the German is complete without it; the bracketed [go] is supplied by this edition, not by the German, so the English can stand. halb and ganz follow their noun like adverbs — the kingdom half now, whole later.

sentences.t: „So wünsch ich daß der gute Anfang auch ein gutes Ende nehme“ sprach der Jüngling, „ich bleibe bei euch.“
sentences.l: “So wish I that the good beginning may also take a good end” spoke the youth, “I stay with you.”
sentences.i: “Then I wish that the good beginning may take a good end too,” said the young man; “I will stay with you.”
sentences.n: “ein Ende nehmen” = to come to an end, and nehme is subjunctive after wünschen: the wish, not the fact. wünsch drops its -e as speech does. euch is the respectful address he owes the old king.

sentences.t: Da gab ihm der Alte das halbe Reich, und als er nach einem Jahr starb, hatte er das ganze, und nach dem Tod seines Vaters noch eins dazu, und lebte in aller Herrlichkeit.
sentences.l: Then gave him the old man the half kingdom, and when he died after a year, he had the whole, and after the death of his father one more besides, and lived in all splendour.
sentences.i: Then the old man gave him half the kingdom, and when he died a year later he had it whole, and after his own father’s death one more besides, and lived in all splendour.
sentences.n: The er of “als er … starb” is the old king, and the er just after it is the young one — German lets a pronoun change hands without warning and leaves the sense to sort them out. eins is one more kingdom: the one he was born to. The tale closes on the formula and says nothing more about the burnt skin.

glossary.alter: alt — old (masc. inflected; ein alter König, an old king)
glossary.angst: die Angst — fear, dread (voll Trauer und Angst, full of grief and fear)
glossary.anstellen: sich anstellen — to behave, to take a thing (infinitive; ‘wie er sich anstellen würde’, how he would take it; anstellen alone = to set up, arrange)
glossary.betragen: sich betragen — to conduct oneself, to behave (infinitive; the same form serves as past participle)
glossary.drehte: drehen — turned (3rd sg. past; den Kopf drehen, to turn the head)
glossary.eingehen: eingehen — to go in, to enter (infinitive; separable ein-)
glossary.eins: eins — one (neuter; noch eins dazu, one more besides)
glossary.erbe: der Erbe — heir (masc.; das Erbe, neuter, is the inheritance itself)
glossary.es: es — it (it also stands for a person named by a neuter noun: das Eselein is es, “it,” for most of this tale)
glossary.gefällt: gefallen — pleases (wie gefällt dir …, how do you like …, with the person in the dative)
glossary.gerade: gerade — just, exactly (das wars gerade, that was the very thing)
glossary.gutem: gut — good (dat. sg.; in gutem Muth, in good spirits)
glossary.hieß: heißen — bade, ordered (3rd sg. past; jemandem etwas heißen, to bid someone do a thing; heißen also means to be called)
glossary.ja: ja — yes; inside a sentence also an unstressed particle, surely, after all (du schaust ja sauer)
glossary.junges: jung — young (adj., neuter inflected: ein junges Eselein; the noun das Junge means a young one, a cub)
glossary.lehre: lehren — teach (imperative sg.; ‘lehre mich’, teach me; the noun die Lehre means a lesson)
glossary.lust: die Lust — pleasure, delight (seine Lust an etwas haben, to take one’s delight in a thing; also desire, appetite)
glossary.manierlich: manierlich — mannerly, well-mannered (adverb with sich betragen)
glossary.reich: reich — rich (adjective); also das Reich — kingdom, realm (noun)
glossary.setze: sich setzen — seat yourself, sit down (imperative sg.: ‘setze dich’; also 1st sg. ich setze)
glossary.sorge: sorgen — I fear, I am afraid (1st sg. present; ‘ich sorge …’, I am afraid that …; the noun die Sorge means care, worry)
glossary.sperrte: aufsperren — opened wide (3rd sg. past with separable auf-: ‘sperrte die Augen auf’; sperren by itself means to shut, to bar)
glossary.tragen: tragen — to carry; also to wear (die Krone tragen) and to bring in, to yield (a return)
glossary.wacht: wachen — keep watch (2nd pl. imperative; ‘so wacht selber’, then keep watch yourself; the noun die Wacht means a watch, a guard)
glossary.wünsche: der Wunsch — wishes (pl.; the same spelling is also wünsche, I wish, from wünschen)
glossary.zogen: ziehen — travelled, journeyed (3rd pl. past; ‘sie zogen auf und ab’, they wandered up and down; ziehen also means to pull)
